name: Felix Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Felix. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI firms, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential and won't be tied to your name. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on a hospital refurbishment, the old outpatients wing, so it's a strange one because the hospital's still running next door. I do interior fit-out: metal stud walls, plasterboard, door frames and doors, ceiling grids, boxing in pipes. We start at seven, and everything's dust sheets and permits, because you can't just make noise when there's a clinic on the other side of a temporary wall. I'm with the same contractor nine years now, and I eat lunch with Kofi, our electrician, in his van because it's got a heater.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is hanging doors, weirdly. A fire door that closes properly, flush, with the right gaps all round, is a small thing nobody notices, and I love it. Worst is the paperwork for every hole you cut, and redoing a wall because the design team moved a socket by twenty centimetres after it was boarded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and get back to my door frames. I don't think I'd post anything. Maybe I'd send Kofi a message saying he owes me a coffee, because he was sure the robots were coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it wouldn't change much for me. I've used one of those chatbots a few times, once to explain a fire-door rule I didn't understand and once to help Ines write a letter to the council about the bins. If that's all it ever is, a handy helper, I'm fine with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Same contractor, same savings habit, which is a set amount on payday that I never touch. We'd probably go ahead with the loft conversion, we've been putting money aside for it for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to feel much about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kofi was sure the robots were coming. What was he expecting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd seen one of those layout robots, a little machine that drives around an empty floor and draws all the wall lines from the drawings in chalk or ink. It's quite clever, to be fair. He thought within a few years it'd be doing the walls as well, not just drawing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want something like that layout robot on your sites, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once it's proven, sure. Marking out a floor takes two of us most of a day, and if a machine does it overnight and gets it right, I'll happily skip the kneeling. I just wouldn't want to be the first site to try it, because the first one is always the one that breaks.

S0.say: I'd say that's that, then, and get back to my door frames without posting anything. Maybe I'd message Kofi that he owes me a coffee, since he was sure the robots were coming.
S0.think: Privately it wouldn't change much, because he only uses chatbots now and then, like checking a fire-door rule or helping with a letter to the council. If AI stays a handy helper, he's comfortable with that.
S0.do: Carries on with the same contractor and keeps putting a fixed sum into savings every payday. Goes ahead with the loft conversion the family has saved toward for two years.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing much to worry about.
S0.quote: I just wouldn't want to be the first site to try it, because the first one is always the one that breaks.
S0.fieldNote: Felix is a classic 'second adopter': open to tools once someone else has ironed out the problems. His pleasure in small, precise work like a well-hung fire door is a real part of who he is. The plateau changes nothing in his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine as long as the gains are shared, which is what I'd always say. If machines do more of the work, the people left should get a shorter week or better pay, not just the shareholders. I'd say that to Kofi and probably at a union meeting, though I'm not a big speaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think fit-out changes but doesn't vanish. Already half our bathrooms come in as ready-made pods on a lorry, and someone still has to fit them, connect them and fix the walls around them. Hospitals are full of awkward old corners, and I can't picture a machine dealing with a 1970s ceiling void full of asbestos labels and surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch which tools the bigger sites start using, and once two or three of the crew say it works, I'd ask the contractor to put me on the training. I'd probably get better at using the chatbot for reading specs and checking rules, which saves me ringing the site manager. Otherwise I'd keep going and keep saving like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little curious, a little wary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plasterers, maybe, because big flat walls are just the kind of thing a machine can spray and smooth. And the apprentices. If the easy jobs go to machines, where does an eighteen-year-old learn the trade? You learn by doing the boring stuff for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try new tools first. Is there any risk in being late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. But I've got savings, there's plenty of fit-out work in this area, and the people who go first tend to tell you everything that went wrong. I'd rather be six months behind and still have my weekends than be the guinea pig.

S1.say: I'd say it's fine as long as the gains are shared, with a shorter week or better pay rather than everything going to shareholders. I'd say it to Kofi and maybe at a union meeting, though I'm not a big speaker.
S1.think: Privately he thinks fit-out will change but not vanish, since bathroom pods already arrive ready-made and still need fitting. He can't picture a machine dealing with an old hospital ceiling void full of surprises.
S1.do: Watches which tools bigger sites adopt and asks for training once colleagues report they work. Uses the chatbot more for reading specs and checking rules, and otherwise keeps working and saving as before.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, a little curious and a little wary.
S1.quote: I'd rather be six months behind and still have my weekends than be the guinea pig.
S1.fieldNote: Felix's progressive views show in his first instinct, that productivity gains should be shared, but he isn't an organiser. His worry jumps quickly to apprentices and how the trade gets passed on. Savings and plentiful local work let him wait comfortably for proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in, fast, with some kind of income for people whose work disappears. If a company replaces fifty carpenters with ten robots, it should be taxed for it, simple as that. I'd say it at the union and I'd probably share posts about it, which I never normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared, but not flat on my back. Ines is a children's nurse and I honestly can't see a parent handing their sick five-year-old to a robot, so I think her job holds longer than mine. Between her wage and our savings, about nine months of everything, we'd be squeezed but not sunk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the loft conversion straight away and keep that money as cash. We'd cut the second car and the summer holiday, which saves a fair bit. Work-wise, I'd keep going as long as there's work, and I'd wait to see the robots actually turn up on a site before I did anything drastic, because I've heard a lot of predictions in my time. And I'd go to the union meetings properly, not just pay the dues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be in control but worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loft, which was going to be Oskar's bedroom so he and Nora stop fighting. Then my football season ticket, which hurts more than I'd like to admit. Then probably the second car, because Ines can cycle to the hospital in summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see robots on site before doing anything drastic. But you'd also cancel the loft straight away. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, fair. I suppose the money stuff I'd do on day one, because that's cheap and you can undo it. Throwing away nine years with my contractor and starting over somewhere, that I'd only do once I'd seen it with my own eyes.

S2.say: I'd say governments must step in fast with income for people whose work disappears, and companies replacing workers with robots should be taxed for it. I'd share posts about it, which I never usually do.
S2.think: Privately he'd be scared but not floored, because he thinks his wife's job as a children's nurse will last longer than his. Her wage plus about nine months of savings means squeezed but not sunk.
S2.do: Cancels the loft conversion on day one and keeps that money as cash, drops the second car, the summer holiday and his football season ticket. Keeps working while waiting to see robots on site before any big career move, and starts going to union meetings properly.
S2.feel: Anxious, but still feeling in control.
S2.quote: I honestly can’t see a parent handing their sick five-year-old to a robot, so I think her job holds longer than mine.
S2.fieldNote: His sense of safety rests heavily on his wife's nursing job, which he assumes is protected; that assumption carries a lot of weight. He reconciled the contradiction neatly: cheap, reversible money moves now, big career moves only once he sees proof. The season ticket admission was a nice human touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so let's use the time. Tax the machines, pay for retraining, keep apprenticeships going. I'd say that in the union and I'd vote for whoever has an actual plan, not just a slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a choice I wouldn't have with two. Ines keeps saying people will always want a person at the bedside, and the hospital I'm working in now is short of everything, porters, estates staff, healthcare assistants. I think I'd look at moving into hospital estates, the in-house maintenance team, where I'd still use my hands but be part of the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the estates manager at the hospital, I've met him a few times on this job, and ask what they look for. If it meant an evening course in building services or maintenance, I'd do it in the second or third year once I saw which way it was going. Meanwhile the loft gets postponed, not cancelled, and the extra goes into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing weather coming but having an umbrella.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take that step, rather than staying put?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first robots doing stud walls on a big site and actually working. Not a video, a real site where someone I know works. Kofi has a cousin at one of the big contractors, so I'd hear about it soon enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Oskar, who's fourteen, about his own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to do something with computers, games or whatever. I'd tell him to keep at it but to learn something with people in it too. I don't really know what's safe, to be honest, and I wouldn't pretend to him that I do.

S3.say: I'd say we've been warned, so we should use the time to tax the machines, pay for retraining and keep apprenticeships going. I'd vote for whoever has an actual plan, not a slogan.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years gives him a real choice, and he'd look at moving into the hospital's in-house maintenance team. His wife's view that people want a person at the bedside shapes where he sees safety.
S3.do: Talks to the hospital's estates manager about what they look for and would take an evening course in building services in the second or third year if things move. Postpones the loft and puts the extra into savings.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like seeing weather coming with an umbrella in hand.
S3.quote: Like seeing weather coming but having an umbrella.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Felix's steady style turns into a concrete plan: a move into hospital estates, triggered by seeing robots work on a real site. He's honest that he doesn't know what's safe for his son. His politics show mostly at the ballot box, not in activism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to do it properly, so no excuses. Retraining money, protection for older workers, a tax on companies that replace people. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, and I'd vote that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is almost comfortable. I'd be fifty-three, Oskar and Nora would be through school, and the mortgage would be a lot smaller. I'd still lose my trade, probably, but I'd have time to slide into something else rather than be thrown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing fit-out for a good few years and keep saving. Somewhere around year three or four I'd do that building services course and try to get onto the hospital estates team. And we'd do the loft after all, because it adds value to the house and Oskar's waited long enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a little knot in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the knot about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids. I'd have my bit sorted, but Nora's ten and I don't know what her world looks like at twenty. And Ines, if she's wrong about the bedside, then we're both out together, and that's the one I don't let myself think about for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having more time change anything about the loft decision you made in the faster pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. With two years, cash is king. With ten, the loft's a good investment and a happier house. And you can't spend a decade with two kids fighting over one bedroom.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is enough to do this properly, so there are no excuses. He'd push for retraining money, protection for older workers and a tax on companies replacing people, and vote that way.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels almost comfortable, with the kids through school and the mortgage smaller by the time he's fifty-three. He expects to lose his trade but slide into something else rather than be thrown out.
S4.do: Keeps working in fit-out and saving for several years, then does a building services course around year three or four and aims for the hospital estates team. Goes ahead with the loft conversion as an investment in the house.
S4.feel: Mostly settled, with a small knot of worry about the kids and his wife.
S4.quote: With two years, cash is king. With ten, the loft's a good investment and a happier house.
S4.fieldNote: Felix's loft conversion became a neat gauge of his confidence across the pictures: cancelled, postponed, then built. He let slip the one fear he avoids, that his wife's job might not be safe either. The longer timeline suits his wait-for-proof temperament well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because we'd starve, we wouldn't, but because there's no time to see it working before you have to decide, and that's how I make decisions. What would help is a clear government plan up front: an income for people whose trade goes, paid partly by the companies, and free retraining for jobs that actually exist, not courses for the sake of courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the buildings. I've spent nine years in hospitals and schools, and they're falling apart because there's never money. If machines make things cheaper, I'd love some of it to go into fixing them. If it just goes into somebody's yacht, then what was the point of all those clever robots?

headlineQuote: If it just goes into somebody's yacht, then what was the point of all those clever robots?
portrait: Felix is a 43-year-old fit-out carpenter on a hospital refurbishment, steady and practical, who uses chatbots now and then and likes to let others test new tools first. His wife is a children's nurse, and her job, which he believes will outlast his, plus nine months of savings, is the floor under his family. He stays calm in the plateau and steady pictures, gets anxious when AGI comes in two years and moves money straight away while waiting for proof before changing careers. With five or ten years he plans a move into the hospital's in-house maintenance team, and his loft conversion goes from cancelled to built as the warning time grows.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to see changes work before having to decide, which is how he likes to make choices.
whatWouldHelp: A clear government plan in advance: income for people whose trade disappears, paid partly by the companies, and free retraining for jobs that really exist.
